physical_harm: The deceased's body was found partly eaten out by aquatic animals with injuries consistent with homicidal attack
number_of_offences: Two offences/counts charged, one finally upheld
premeditation_planning: The court found premeditation/planning based on motive and chain of circumstances
motive: Frequent fights between the deceased and the appellant and his second wife
key_evidence_accepted: The circumstances stated by the trial court and concretized by the High Court, namely, the deceased and the accused were last seen together on 06.12.2001, the body of the deceased was recovered at the instance of the appellant, the recovery of the knife by the police from the place of occurrence, the frequent quarrels between the deceased and the accused, the theory of the deceased having run away from the matrimonial home not properly explained by the appellant, the weapon used containing blood stains, the nature of injuries found on the body of the deceased, the post mortem doctor's opinion that the death was homicidal, the appellant wanting to flee from the town, and the clothes seized from the appellant containing human blood.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that the circumstances were fully established and consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the appellant, and that the facts were not explainable on any other hypothesis except that the accused was guilty.
post_offence_conduct: The appellant wanted to flee from the town itself and was in the process of leaving the village with his family, which led to his apprehension by the police.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 6.12.2001; Trial judgment: 25 & 28.11.2005; High Court decision: 24.04.2008; Supreme Court decision: 26.07.2012
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Gopal Prasad; Counsel for the State: Sachin Pitale (for Asha Gopalan Nair)
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted; High Court: Acquitted A-2, maintained conviction of appellant; Supreme Court: Dismissed appeal
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant and his brother were seen with the deceased on 6.12.2001, their clothes were blood-stained, the appellant claimed the deceased had run away, and the body was recovered at the instance of the appellant. The knife used was found with blood stains, and the post-mortem report indicated the death was homicidal.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the body of the deceased was found in a decomposed state, half eaten by aquatic animals, making identification uncertain. They also pointed out missing links in the chain of circumstances and claimed the appellant did not dispute the identity of the body.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that in cases of circumstantial evidence, the circumstances must be fully established, consistent only with the hypothesis of the accused's guilt, conclusive in nature, and exclude every other hypothesis except that the accused is guilty.
precedent_relied_upon: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra 1984 (4) SCC 116; Shivaji Sahabrao Bobade v. State of Maharashtra 1973 (2) SCC 793; Hanumant Govind Nargundkar & Anr. v. State of Madhya Pradesh AIR 1952 SC 343; Naseem Ahmed v. Delhi Administration 1974 (3) SCC 668; Rukia Begum & Ors. v. State of Karnataka 2011 (4) SCC 779; Prithipal Singh & Ors v. State of Punjab 2012 (1) SCC 10
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the circumstances were consistent with the hypothesis of the appellant's guilt, the motive and chain of circumstances proved against him, and the evidence was conclusive and excluded every other hypothesis.
